senses.definition: Ellipsis of fly route.
A piece of canvas that covers the opening at the front of a tent.
senses.example: We zipped the fly shut to keep the mosquitoes out of the tent.

senses.definition: A strip of material (sometimes hiding zippers or buttons) at the front of a pair of trousers, pants, underpants, bootees, etc.
senses.example: Ha-ha! Your fly's undone!

senses.definition: The moving portion of an extendable ladder.
senses.example: The fly of the extension ladder slid up with a loud clank.

senses.definition: The free edge of a flag.
senses.example: Wind caught the fly of the flag and snapped it out straight over the porch.

senses.definition: The horizontal length of a flag.
senses.example: The flag's fly measured twelve feet, so it filled the pole nicely.

senses.definition: An exercise that involves wide opening and closing of the arms perpendicular to the shoulders.
senses.example: The physical therapist had me do arm flies to strengthen my shoulders after surgery.

senses.definition: The part of a weather vane pointing the direction from which the wind blows.
senses.example: The fly of the weather vane swung toward the north as the storm approached.

senses.definition: Two or more vanes set on a revolving axis, to act as a fanner, or to equalize or impede the motion of machinery by the resistance of the air, as in the striking part of a clock.
senses.example: The fly on the clock's striking mechanism slowed the hammer so the chime wouldn't rush.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of flywheel.
In a knitting machine, the piece hinged to the needle, which holds the engaged loop in position while the needle is penetrating another loop; a latch.
senses.example: The fly on the knitting machine held each loop steady while the needle moved through.

senses.definition: The pair of arms revolving around the bobbin, in a spinning wheel or spinning frame, to twist the yarn.
A shuttle driven through the shed by a blow or jerk.
The person who took the printed sheets from the press.
A vibrating frame with fingers, attached to a power printing press for doing the same work.
One of the upper screens of a stage in a theater.
Waste cotton.
A fly ball.
That part of a compass on which the points are marked; the compass card.
(historical) A type of small, light, fast horse-drawn carriage that can be hired for transportation (sometimes pluralized flys).
senses.example: Related terms: flyman
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To travel through the air, another gas, or a vacuum, without being in contact with a grounded surface.
senses.example: Birds of passage fly to warmer regions as it gets colder in winter.

senses.definition: To take a flight on a plane; to pilot or crew a plane.
senses.example: My airline needs me to get clearance before I can fly again.

senses.definition: To be accepted, come about or work out.
senses.example: Let's see if that idea flies.

senses.definition: To cause to fly (travel or float in the air): to transport via air or the like.
senses.example: Charles Lindbergh flew his airplane The Spirit of St. Louis across the Atlantic ocean.

senses.definition: To arrange for someone to take a flight.
senses.example: We flew the kids out to see their grandparents.

senses.definition: To pilot a plane over a region or on a route.
senses.example: This is the first time I flew the Pacific.

senses.definition: To complete (a goal, task, mission, etc.) while crewing an aircraft or spacecraft.
To hunt with a hawk.
To wave or flutter; to cause to wave or flutter.
senses.example: When the wind picked up, her hair flew back behind her head.

senses.definition: To operate a kite (A lightweight toy or other device. carried on the wind and tethered and controlled from the ground by one or more lines).
senses.example: Why don’t you go outside and fly kites, kids? The wind is just perfect.

senses.definition: To display (a flag) on a flagpole; to be displayed on a flagpole.
senses.example: We flew the state flag under the national flag.

senses.definition: To proudly and openly make one's allegiances or viewpoint apparent.
senses.example: She's really letting the freak flag fly.

senses.definition: To symbolically rule over or control.
senses.example: The French flag flew over Louisiana until 1803.

senses.definition: To drain away or be expended quickly.
senses.example: The family fortune flew in a few short years.

senses.definition: To travel or proceed very fast; to hasten.
senses.example: He flew down the hill on his bicycle.

senses.definition: To move suddenly, or with violence; to carry out an act suddenly or swiftly.
senses.example: a door flies open

senses.definition: To proceed with great success.
senses.example: His career is really flying at the moment.

senses.definition: To be in the winged adult stage.
senses.example: This species flies from late summer until frost.

senses.definition: To hit a fly ball; to hit a fly ball that is caught for an out. Compare ground (verb) and line (verb).
senses.example: Jones flied to right in his last at-bat.

senses.definition: (dated) To vanish; to fade away.
senses.example: The mist flew by noon.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Clandestine, surreptitious.
Well dressed, smart in appearance; in style, cool.
senses.example: He's pretty fly.

senses.definition: Beautiful; displaying physical beauty.
(dated) Quick-witted, alert, mentally sharp.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A small winged insect, such as a housefly, belonging to the order Diptera; Americans often call any small flying insect a fly or a bug.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a diphthong that glides from 'ah' to 'ee'; finish with a clear 'ee' sound and do not add an extra vowel. The noun and the verb 'to fly' sound exactly the same.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general, but negative when the insect is in food or near people, where it is annoying or unsanitary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fly for the housefly and similar insects, and bug for insects in general, including beetles and spiders. A common restaurant complaint is 'There's a fly in my soup,' which is said calmly but expects a replacement. Most learners use the verb 'to fly' (travel through the air or by plane) more often than the insect noun.

distinctions.note: Bug is the everyday general word for any small insect or creepy-crawly; fly is more specific to flies in the order Diptera.
A mosquito is also a Diptera insect, but it is named for its biting habit and is a separate term in everyday American speech.
A gnat is a very small fly, such as a fruit fly or fungus gnat, and is used for tiny flying insects.

examples.everyday: There's a fly buzzing around the kitchen, so could you grab the swatter?
examples.professional: The fruit fly colony in the lab needs to be checked before Monday's trial.
examples.analytical: The fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, has long served as a model organism in genetic research.

nuance.analogy: A fly is like a buzzing thought that keeps returning no matter how many times you wave it away.
nuance.etymology: From Old English flēoge, from a Germanic root related to the verb fly.
common_mistakes: Using 'flys' as the plural; the plural is 'flies'.
Calling a beetle or spider a fly; Americans would say bug for those.
Pronouncing the vowel as a short 'i' like 'flih'; it is a long diphthong.

fly.etymology: From Middle English *fflye*, *flehe*, *flei*, *fleie*, *fley*, *fleye*, *fleȝe*, *flie*, *fliȝe*, *flye*, *vliȝe*, *vlye*, from Old English *flēge*, *flēoge*, *flīeġe* (“a fly”), from **fleugā*, from Proto-Germanic **fleugǭ* (“a fly”), from…

senses.definition: A man in waiting; a male servant whose duties are to attend the door, the carriage, the table, etc.
A metallic stand with four feet, for keeping anything warm before a fire.
senses.example: We warmed the bread on the iron footman beside the hearth before serving dinner.

senses.definition: A moth of the family Arctiidae (or subfamily Arctiinae); so called from its livery-like colors.
senses.example: A small footman moth fluttered around the porch light, its bright yellow wings marked with dark stripes.

senses.definition: Especially, a common footman (Manulea lurideola).
senses.example: The common footman is a drab moth whose larvae feed on lichens growing on old stone walls.

senses.definition: A bar that connects the treadle of a spinning wheel to the wheel.
senses.example: The footman on my great-grandmother's spinning wheel snapped, so the treadle no longer turned the wheel.

senses.definition: (historical) A servant who runs in front of his master's carriage.
senses.example: The footman hurried ahead of the carriage, clearing the crowd so the duchess could pass safely.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A male servant in a wealthy household, in uniform, who opens doors and attends guests at a carriage or table.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FUT. The final syllable is a reduced 'mun', not 'man' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly formal. It describes a historical or period role, often with a sense of old-fashioned class structure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'footman' today, except in historical fiction, period dramas, or discussions of Victorian households. In modern American life, the closest words are 'doorman' for a building attendant or 'butler' for a household servant. You might hear it in a British period drama or a museum tour.

distinctions.note: A butler manages the household and its staff; a footman is a lower servant who attends the door, carriage, or table.
A doorman works at a building entrance; a footman is a historical household servant, not a modern job.

examples.everyday: In that old British series, the footman always wore white gloves and opened the carriage door.
examples.professional: Our historical society is restoring the mansion, including the uniforms worn by the footmen.
examples.analytical: The novel uses the footman as a symbol of the rigid hierarchy that separates the servants from the family.

nuance.analogy: A footman is like a living doorway: he is present to open and guide, but he does not make the decisions.
nuance.etymology: From 'foot' and 'man', originally a man who went on foot beside or before a carriage.
common_mistakes: Assuming 'footman' is a common modern job title in the US; it is mainly historical.
Confusing 'footman' with 'footmen' pronunciation or spelling in the plural.

footman.etymology: From Middle English *fotman*, *footman*, *foteman* (“foot soldier, running footman”), from Old English **fōtman*, **fōtmann* (attested only as, *fēþemann* (“footman”), equivalent to *foot* + *man*.

senses.definition: Covered in forest.

core.definition: Covered with trees; having a lot of forest growing on it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on FOR. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, so say it like FOR-uh-stid, not FOR-est-ed with a full vowel in each syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it is often used to describe scenery, land, or property in a way that sounds pleasant or natural.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use forested in everyday talk about landscapes, road trips, and real estate, such as a heavily forested mountain. It is a plain descriptive word and sounds natural in spoken English. For areas with few trees, use wooded, treeless, or cleared instead.

distinctions.note: Wooded is the more casual, everyday word for having trees; forested usually suggests a larger, denser area covered by forest.
Forest is a noun for the large tree-covered area itself; forested is the adjective describing land that has one.

examples.everyday: We drove through heavily forested hills all the way to the lake.
examples.professional: The survey flagged the forested parcels as needing a separate habitat assessment before construction.
examples.analytical: The poem imagines a forested landscape as a space where the mind can return to itself.

nuance.analogy: A forested area is like a crowded room full of tall people: the trees are everywhere you look.
nuance.etymology: From forest (noun) plus the adjective ending -ed, meaning covered with a forest.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ed as a separate syllable, as in FOR-es-ted, when the normal American form is FOR-uh-stid.
Using forested to describe a single small group of trees; wooded or tree-lined is more natural for that.

senses.definition: To pardon (someone); to waive any negative feeling towards or desire for punishment or retribution against.
senses.example: Please forgive me if my phone goes off - I'm expecting an urgent call from my boss.

senses.definition: To pardon (something); to waive any negative feeling over or retribution for.
senses.example: I forgive you for missing my birthday, but please don't do it again.

senses.definition: To waive or remit (a debt), to absolve from payment or compensation of.
senses.example: Forgive a debt, that is, tell a debtor that a repayment of a loan is no longer needed.

senses.definition: To accord forgiveness.
senses.example: Her grandmother was quick to forgive, even after years of bitter arguments.

senses.definition: To look past; to look beyond.
senses.example: The music critic loves the instrumentation of the song so much that he can forgive the confusing lyrics.

senses.definition: To redeem; to offset the bad effects of something.
senses.example: No amount of overtime could forgive the damage his careless code had done.

core.definition: To stop feeling angry toward someone for a wrong they did and give up the desire to punish or repay them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, GIV, and keep the first syllable weak like 'fur'. The short i in GIV is like the vowel in 'give', not 'five'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Forgiving is generally admired, though the word can be heavy when it is used for serious wrongs.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use forgive in everyday apologies, such as 'Forgive me for being late,' which is a polite formula. It is also common in church, counseling, and family conversation. A natural reply to an apology is 'You're forgiven' or 'Don't worry about it.' For small mistakes, Americans often say no problem rather than forgive me.

distinctions.note: Pardon usually refers to an official legal release from punishment, while forgive is personal and emotional.
Excuse is used for small social mistakes, such as excuse me, while forgive is used for real wrongs or hurts.

examples.everyday: I'm sorry I forgot your birthday, will you forgive me?
examples.professional: We agreed to forgive the late invoice fee this time, but it needs to be on time going forward.
examples.analytical: Paul's letters present God as one who forgives sinners through grace, not through the sinner's merit.

nuance.analogy: To forgive is like canceling a debt in your own ledger: you still know what was owed, but you choose not to collect it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English forgiefan, from for- (completely, away) and giefan (to give).
common_mistakes: Using forgive for minor social slips where excuse or no problem sounds more natural.
Confusing forgive with forget. Forgiving means releasing anger toward a person; forgetting means losing memory.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, forgiveness is God's act of pardoning sin and restoring a relationship. Hebrew uses nasa, to lift or bear away, as in Psalm 32:1. Greek uses aphiemi, to send away or let go, used in the Lord's Prayer and in Matthew 6:14-15, where forgiving others is linked to receiving forgiveness. Psalm 103:3 praises the LORD who forgives all iniquity, and Ephesians 4:32 calls believers to forgive one another as God forgave them in Christ.

traditions.view: Forgiveness is received within the Church through repentance, confession to a priest in the Mystery of Repentance, and God's mercy, leading to healing and communion with God.
Sins are forgiven in baptism and, after baptism, through the sacrament of Reconciliation, where contrition, confession to a priest, and absolution restore grace.

Forgiveness is God's free pardon received by faith in Christ. Lutherans may retain private absolution, while Reformed and Baptist churches usually emphasize the Gospel declaration of forgiveness without sacramental confession as required.

forgive.etymology: Alteration (due to *give*) of Middle English *foryiven*, *forȝiven*, from Old English *forġiefan* (“to forgive, to give”), from **frageban*, from Proto-Germanic **fragebaną* (“to give away; give up; release; forgive”), equivalent to *for-* + *give*…

senses.definition: To absolve somebody completely for a past wrongdoing; to pardon with neither resentment nor a view to retribution.

core.definition: To pardon someone completely for a wrong, so that you neither hold a grudge nor keep bringing it up.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the two main verbs, GIV and GET, and reduce and to 'und'. Keep the first syllable of each verb weak, like 'fur', so the phrase sounds smooth.

nuance.connotation: Positive in principle, but it can sound dismissive if used to pressure someone to stop talking about a real harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say forgive and forget in relationships, workplaces, or family conflicts, usually as an ideal. The phrase is also a bit of a cliche, and some people say it is easier said than done. A natural reply is 'I'm working on it' or 'Thanks for understanding.'

distinctions.note: Forgive alone means release resentment; forgive and forget adds the idea of fully moving past the event.
Let bygones be bygones is a looser, more relaxed idiom about dropping old disputes, while forgive and forget carries a stronger moral idea.

examples.everyday: We had a big fight last year, but we decided to forgive and forget and go back to being friends.
examples.professional: The team agreed to forgive and forget the missed deadlines, but everyone is now tracking progress more closely.
examples.analytical: Jeremiah's promise that God will forgive and remember sin no more suggests a remembrance that is restorative rather than punitive.

nuance.analogy: Forgiving and forgetting is like erasing a chalkboard after a lesson: the words are removed so the next lesson can begin.
common_mistakes: Saying forgive and forget as if it always means erasing the memory. The phrase usually means releasing resentment, not forgetting the facts.
Using it in a formal context for serious crimes, where forgiveness and legal consequences are separate matters.
nuance.biblical_note: The idea behind forgive and forget is connected to God's promise in Jeremiah 31:34 to forgive iniquity and remember sin no more. In the Hebrew sense, God's remembrance is not mere memory loss but a decision not to hold the sin against His people. The phrase itself is not a biblical quotation.

senses.definition: A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town; for example a fort, a castle; a stronghold; a place of defense or security.
senses.example: The medieval fortress guarded the valley for three centuries before falling to invading armies.

senses.definition: A position that, if obtained by the weaker side, will prevent penetration by the opposing side, generally achieving a draw.
senses.example: Black held a fortress in the endgame, so the rook ending was a draw.

senses.definition: To furnish with a fortress or with fortresses; to guard, to fortify.
senses.example: They fortressed the border town with walls, towers, and garrisons.

core.definition: A large, permanent stronghold built to defend a place against attack, or a place that offers strong protection.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on FOR. The vowel in the first syllable is a clear 'or', and the -tr- blends into a short 'triss' with no extra vowel between the t and r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests safety and strength, but in figurative use it can suggest a closed or defensive attitude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fortress for historic castles, military strongholds, and in figurative talk about something that is hard to get into, such as 'a fortress of privacy'. In everyday speech, they might say a castle, fort, or stronghold. It is a common and natural word in both casual and formal contexts.

distinctions.note: A fort is usually smaller and often military. A fortress is larger and more permanent, often with walls around a town.
A castle is a noble residence and defense, often medieval. A fortress is primarily defensive and may not be a home.

examples.everyday: We drove past an old stone fortress on the hill, and my kids wanted to climb the walls.
examples.professional: The security team treats the server room as a fortress, with badge access and cameras at every door.
examples.analytical: Augustine uses the image of the City of God as a fortress that cannot be taken by the forces of the earthly city.

nuance.analogy: Think of a fortress as a strong wall around a garden: it keeps out the danger, but it also shapes what is inside.
nuance.etymology: From Old French forteresse, from fort (strong), from Latin fortis.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as 'for-TRESS' with the stress on the wrong syllable.
Confusing fortress with fort: a fort is often a smaller military structure, while fortress usually names a larger stronghold.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word misgab, meaning high place or stronghold, is used for God as a fortress for the psalmist. Psalm 18:2 calls the LORD a rock, a fortress, and a deliverer. Psalm 31:3 says God is a rock and a fortress for the one who prays, which Christians read as God's protection of his people.

fortress.etymology: Early 14 c. from Old French *forteresce* (“strong place, fortification”), variant of *fortelesse*, from Medieval Latin *fortalitia*, from Latin *fortis* (“strong”) (see *fort*)*itia*, added to adjectives to form nouns of quality or condition. from is…

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or produced by animals that are allowed to roam freely, rather than being confined indoors.
senses.example: We buy free-range eggs from a farm where hens roam outdoors during the day.

senses.definition: Allowed to move about outdoors without supervision.
senses.example: free-range children

senses.definition: Relating to a hands-off parenting style in which children are allowed to go out and explore alone.
senses.example: free-range parents

core.definition: Describing animals, especially poultry or livestock, raised outdoors and allowed to roam rather than kept in cages or pens.

pronunciation.tip: Stress RAYNJ, with 'free' lighter. The vowel in 'range' is a long diphthong, rhyming with 'change', not a short a.

nuance.connotation: Positive in food marketing and parenting talk, since it suggests animal welfare or independence, though some labels are loosely regulated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see 'free-range' on egg and chicken labels in grocery stores. The USDA sets some rules for poultry, but the label does not guarantee much outdoor space. In parenting talk, 'free-range kids' means children allowed to explore on their own. A natural reply to a question is 'Yes, they're free-range, so the hens get outside.'

distinctions.note: Cage-free birds are not in cages but may still be kept indoors, whereas free-range birds have some outdoor access.
Organic describes feed and chemical rules, while free-range describes the animal's living space.
Pasture-raised is a more specific claim that the animals spend time on grass, which is often stronger than free-range.

examples.everyday: I buy free-range eggs at the farmers market because the hens actually get to go outside.
examples.professional: Our procurement team needs a supplier who can document free-range certification for every contract.
examples.analytical: The free-range label promises more than the regulations guarantee, which invites scrutiny of what outdoor access really means.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog let off the leash in a big park instead of kept in a small yard.
nuance.etymology: Free from Old English freo, and range from Anglo-French rangier 'to put in order', later 'to roam'.
common_mistakes: Omitting the hyphen before a noun: write 'free-range eggs', not 'free range eggs'.
Confusing free-range with cage-free, which describes a different level of animal housing.

senses.definition: Newly produced or obtained; recent.
senses.example: He followed the fresh hoofprints to find the deer.

senses.definition: (of food) Not dried, frozen, or spoiled.
senses.example: After taking a beating in the boxing ring, the left side of his face looked like fresh meat.

senses.definition: Invigoratingly cool and refreshing.
senses.example: What a nice fresh breeze.

senses.definition: (of water) Without salt; not saline.
senses.example: After a day at sea it was good to feel the fresh water of the stream.

senses.definition: Rested; not tired or fatigued.
senses.example: After a full night's sleep, I felt fresh enough to tackle the morning's data cleaning.

senses.definition: In a raw or untried state; uncultured; unpracticed.
senses.example: a fresh hand on a ship

senses.definition: Youthful; florid.
senses.example: Her fresh complexion and bright eyes made her look far younger than her sixty years.

senses.definition: Good, fashionable.
senses.example: a fresh pair of sneakers

senses.definition: Rude, cheeky, or inappropriate; presumptuous; disrespectful; forward.
senses.example: No one liked his fresh comments.

senses.definition: Sexually aggressive or forward; prone to caress too eagerly; overly flirtatious.
senses.example: Hey, don't get fresh with me!

senses.definition: (of plant material) Still green and not dried.
senses.example: Pick the basil just before dinner so the leaves stay fresh and green.

senses.definition: Recently; just recently; most recently.
senses.example: We are fresh out of milk.

senses.definition: A rush of water, along a river or onto the land; a flood.
senses.example: A late-spring fresh rushed down the river overnight and washed out the footbridge.

senses.definition: A stream or spring of fresh water.
senses.example: We filled our canteens at a cold fresh that bubbled from under the limestone ledge.

senses.definition: The mingling of fresh water with salt in rivers or bays, as by means of a flood of fresh water flowing toward or into the sea.
senses.example: Oyster beds thrive in the estuary where the river's fresh meets the salt of the bay.

senses.definition: To pack (fish) loosely on ice.
senses.example: On the trawler, we fresh the haddock loosely on ice in the hold to keep it firm.

senses.definition: To flood or dilute an area of salt water with flowing fresh water.
senses.example: Engineers plan to fresh the lagoon with river water to restore its native marsh grasses.

senses.definition: To become stronger.
senses.example: By midnight the wind had begun to fresh, pushing the sloop hard toward the rocks.

senses.definition: To rebore the barrel of a rifle or shotgun.
senses.example: The gunsmith offered to fresh the old shotgun barrel instead of replacing it.

senses.definition: To update.
senses.example: The team plans to fresh the onboarding slides before next quarter's sales meeting.

senses.definition: To freshen up.
senses.example: Before dinner she went upstairs to fresh up and change into a clean blouse.

senses.definition: To renew.
senses.example: After the retreat, the pastor hoped to fresh his congregation's faith in service to others.

senses.definition: Of a dairy cow, to give birth to a calf.
senses.example: The Holstein is due to fresh next week, so we moved her into the maternity pen.

core.definition: Recently made, picked, or produced, and not frozen, canned, stale, or spoiled.

pronunciation.tip: The r is clear at the start, and the vowel is short, as in 'bed'. The sh is a soft, hissing sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests quality, cleanliness, and newness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fresh constantly for food, bread, produce, and fish, and also for new ideas or a clean start. At a grocery store or restaurant, asking 'Is this fresh?' is normal. In casual speech, 'fresh' can also mean rude or too bold, especially for kids, so context matters.

distinctions.note: New means recently created or never used, while fresh often refers to food or air that is pleasantly unspoiled.
Recent is formal and focuses on time, while fresh focuses on quality or condition.

examples.everyday: Can I get a fresh cup of coffee, please? This one tastes old.
examples.professional: We need fresh data from this quarter before we can finalize the forecast.
examples.analytical: A fresh reading of the text can reveal assumptions that earlier generations of scholars took for granted.

nuance.analogy: Fresh food is like a just-opened window: it lets in clean air and keeps everything from going stale.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fersc, meaning not salted or preserved, related to Old Norse ferskr.
common_mistakes: Using fresh to mean 'new' in every case; for a new job, say 'new', not 'fresh', unless you mean a clean start.
Saying 'fresh' with a long vowel, as in 'freesh'.

fresh.etymology: From Middle English *fressh*, from Old English *fersċ* (“fresh, pure, sweet”), from **frisk* (“fresh”), from Proto-Germanic **friskaz* (“fresh”), from Proto-Indo-European **preysk-* (“fresh”).

conversation.text: Is the bread fresh? It smells amazing.
They make the tortillas fresh every morning.
The fish here is always fresh, never frozen.
The bread is fresh out of the oven.
We bought fresh strawberries at the farmers market.
I use fresh garlic, not the jar kind.

senses.definition: The quality of being frowzy.

core.definition: The quality of being frowzy: musty, stale, untidy or unkempt in a dingy, unpleasant way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FROW. The middle syllable 'zi' is short, like 'zih' rather than 'zee', and the ending '-ness' is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something stale, dowdy or neglected, and is rarely used as a compliment.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word that Americans mostly meet in novels, reviews or descriptive writing. In ordinary speech they say 'musty', 'dingy', 'stale' or 'messiness'. Use it only when you want a precise, slightly literary description of a room, a person or a piece of clothing that smells stale and looks worn.

distinctions.note: Messiness is simply disorder, while frowziness adds a stale, musty, dowdy quality.
Dinginess describes drab, dirty-looking surfaces, while frowziness emphasizes stale air, smell and neglect.

examples.everyday: The frowziness of that old couch made me want to open every window in the house.
examples.professional: The facilities survey listed the frowziness of the break room carpet as the top complaint.
examples.analytical: Dickens makes the frowziness of the boardinghouse a moral condition as well as a physical one.

nuance.analogy: Frowziness is a wool sweater that has been worn too long and then stored in a damp closet.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'frowsiness', which is an accepted variant, but then mixing the two forms in the same text.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'frow-ZEE-ness'.

senses.definition: In a fruitful manner; productively.
senses.example: The two teams worked fruitfully together, producing a stronger research proposal than either could have written alone.

core.definition: In a way that produces good results; productively and beneficially.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'FROOT-fuh-lee,' not 'FROOT-foo-lee.' The dictionary's vowel in the middle is not used in General American.

nuance.connotation: Positive: suggests that time or effort was well spent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fruitfully mainly in formal writing and careful speech about work, study, or discussion, like 'The committee met fruitfully.' In everyday speech people prefer 'productively' or 'well.' It often appears with verbs such as discuss, collaborate, and spend.

distinctions.note: Productively stresses output and efficiency; fruitfully stresses that the outcome is worthwhile or beneficial.
Successfully means the intended goal was reached; fruitfully often describes useful results that may be broader or unplanned.

examples.everyday: Let's use the rest of the hour fruitfully and skip the small talk.
examples.professional: Our two teams collaborated fruitfully on the forecasting model after the first month.
examples.analytical: Scripture is read most fruitfully when the reader attends to its historical context as well as its present call.

nuance.analogy: Like a garden in full bloom, where effort turns into a visible harvest.
nuance.etymology: From fruitful plus -ly.
common_mistakes: Using fruitfully in casual talk when you mean productively; it sounds stiff.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'foo' instead of a weak 'fuh.'

senses.definition: Completely developed or formed.
senses.example: We are in the midst of a full-blown crisis.

senses.definition: At the peak of blossom; ripe.
senses.example: The trees in the garden were resplendent with full-blown white gardenias.

senses.definition: Filled with wind; puffed up.
senses.example: The schooner took to sea with full-blown sails.

core.definition: Fully developed and complete, with all the typical features. Often used for a problem or condition that has become serious.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BLOWN, which rhymes with bone. Do not say the final n as a separate sound after a long oh; keep it short and clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing problems, such as a full-blown crisis; neutral or positive when describing a fully formed plan or idea.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use full-blown almost every day for illnesses, arguments, crises, or projects that have gone past the early stage. It is informal to neutral and is often placed before a noun. It is not used for people in a polite way, so avoid it when describing someone's character.

distinctions.note: Complete says nothing is missing, while full-blown adds that something has grown into a developed or severe form.
Outright emphasizes that something is clear and undisguised, while full-blown emphasizes its advanced stage of development.

examples.everyday: My cold turned into a full-blown flu by Tuesday, so I stayed in bed all weekend.
examples.professional: What started as a small bug became a full-blown outage across three data centers before lunch.
examples.analytical: The disagreement did not stay a private dispute; it developed into a full-blown ideological conflict about the nature of authority.

nuance.analogy: Like a bud that opens into a full flower, something full-blown has passed its early stage and is fully visible.
nuance.etymology: Full comes from Old English ful, and blown is the past participle of blow, in the sense of bloom or open, from Old English blowan.
common_mistakes: Using it for something only starting, such as a small idea that has not yet developed.
Pronouncing the vowel in blown like the one in down instead of a long oh sound.
Putting it after the noun; it is normally used before the noun.

senses.definition: Large movable item(s), usually in a room, which enhance(s) the room's characteristics, functionally or decoratively.
senses.example: The woman does not even have one stick of furniture moved in yet.

senses.definition: The harness, trappings etc. of a horse, hawk, or other animal.
senses.example: The saddle, bridle, and other furniture on the mare needed repairs before the ride.

senses.definition: Fittings, such as handles, of a door, coffin, or other wooden item.
senses.example: The carpenter replaced the brass furniture on the cabinet doors.

senses.definition: The stock and forearm of a weapon.
senses.example: The rifle's furniture was worn smooth from years of hunting.

senses.definition: Any material on the page other than the body text and pictures of articles; for example, headlines, datelines and dinkuses, lines and symbols (though in earlier use, only non-text elements of page design, such as lines and symbols).
senses.example: The designer removed the headlines and datelines from the page furniture before sending the proof.

senses.definition: Impressive-looking books used for filling out the collection of a private library.
senses.example: The estate sale included shelves of leather-bound books that were mere furniture.

senses.definition: The stumps.
senses.example: The bowler struck the furniture, and the batsman was out.

senses.definition: A type of mixture organ stop.
senses.example: The organist pulled the furniture stop to add shimmering upper harmonics to the full organ.

senses.definition: (historical) The pieces of wood or metal put around pages of type to make proper margins and fill the spaces between the pages and the chase.
senses.example: Before locking the forme, the printer tightened the furniture around each page.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Large movable items, such as chairs, tables, and beds, that make a room useful or attractive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle and last syllables, so the ending sounds like 'cher', not 'tyoor'. Learners often say three full vowels or stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is ordinary and carries no positive or negative feeling by itself.
nuance.usage_note: Furniture is uncountable in American English, so say 'a piece of furniture' or 'some furniture', never 'a furniture' or 'furnitures'. Americans use it for home and office items, and 'outdoor furniture' and 'office furniture' are common shopping terms. The horse-harness and door-fitting senses in the dictionary are archaic and you will not meet them in daily life.

distinctions.note: Furnishings is broader and includes curtains, rugs, lamps and other decor, while furniture refers mainly to large movable pieces.
Fixtures are attached to a building, such as light fixtures or built-in cabinets, while furniture can be moved from room to room.

examples.everyday: We need to move the couch and the coffee table before the movers get here.
examples.professional: The office furniture order is delayed, so the new team can't move in until next month.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of design often argue that furniture gains its meaning from the daily rituals it supports, not merely from its physical form.

nuance.analogy: Furniture is to a room what a cast is to a play: it gives the space its character and purpose.
nuance.etymology: From Middle French fourniture, from fournir 'to furnish'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a furniture' or 'furnitures' instead of 'a piece of furniture'.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'fur-NIH-cher'.

furniture.etymology: From Middle French *fourniture* (“a supply, or the act of furnishing”), from *fournir* (“to furnish”).

senses.definition: A (usually female) street urchin; a homeless girl.
senses.example: The city shelter found a gamine sleeping under the bridge and offered her a warm bed.

senses.definition: A mischievous, playful, elfish, pert girl or young woman.
Having a boyish, mischievous charm; elfish, typically with short hair.
senses.example: The actress played a gamine heroine with cropped hair and a mischievous grin.

core.definition: A small, playful, boyish-looking girl or young woman with a mischievous, elfish charm.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final vowel is a long ee, not a short i. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or end with a short vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive, with an affectionate tone about a girl's cheeky, spirited charm. It is a compliment and rarely used about adults in a way that sounds insulting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in fashion writing, film criticism, or literary descriptions of a slim, short-haired, playful woman, such as an actress with a pixie look. It is rarely used in everyday conversation. In ordinary speech, say 'pixie' or 'cute and boyish' instead.

distinctions.note: Pixie describes a delicate, elfin look or a short haircut, while gamine adds a boyish, mischievous attitude.
A tomboy is a girl who enjoys boyish activities; gamine emphasizes an elfish, impish charm more than a preference for sports.

examples.everyday: My sister has that gamine look with her short hair and big grin, so people always mistake her for a teenager.
examples.professional: The creative director wanted a gamine look for the spring campaign, so the models wore short cropped hair and playful, boyish clothes.
examples.analytical: Critics have long read the gamine figure in film as a challenge to conventional femininity, combining innocence with a knowing, mischievous independence.

nuance.analogy: A gamine is like a sprite in a children's story: small, quick, and slightly naughty, with a face that looks young and wise at once.
nuance.etymology: From French gamin, meaning street boy or urchin, originally from a dialect word for a playful child.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as GAM-in instead of gam-EEN.
Using gamine for any small girl; it implies a specific playful, boyish charm.
Pronouncing the final vowel as a short i.

senses.definition: A worker who removes refuse, especially from properties.
senses.example: The garbage collector arrives every Tuesday morning before the sun comes up.

senses.definition: An algorithm, procedure or thread dedicated to garbage collection: reclaiming resources which are no longer in use.
senses.example: The garbage collector in our Java application kept pausing the server during peak traffic.

core.definition: A runtime component that automatically finds and frees memory that a program no longer uses.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on LEK in collector. The final -or is a reduced, rhotic syllable (tur), not 'tor.' Many learners pronounce the -ct cluster too weakly; say the k clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In software it is a neutral technical term; for people it is a neutral job title.
nuance.usage_note: Developers say garbage collector for the memory component and often shorten it to GC. For the worker who collects trash, Americans usually say garbage collector, garbage man, or sanitation worker, and the city may call the job waste collection. Be clear which meaning you mean when talking to non-engineers, since the same phrase covers both.

distinctions.note: An allocator grants memory to a program, while a garbage collector reclaims memory that is no longer reachable.
A collector may be a person who gathers stamps or art, but a garbage collector is specifically a person or program that removes unwanted material.

examples.everyday: The garbage collector comes early on Mondays, so put the cans out the night before.
examples.professional: We switched to a generational garbage collector, and our API latency dropped by about 30 percent.
examples.analytical: Describing the garbage collector as a janitor of memory is useful, but it hides the tradeoff between pause time and throughput.

nuance.analogy: Like a night-shift custodian who sweeps up every desk that has been cleared, so the next person finds the room ready.
nuance.etymology: Garbage comes from Anglo-Norman garbage (offal); collector comes from Latin colligere, 'to gather together,' through Anglo-French.
common_mistakes: Using 'garbage collector' for a person who collects things; a person who collects stamps is a collector, not a garbage collector.
Saying 'garbage collector' in a sentence about trash without context, which may confuse a software conversation.

senses.definition: A granary; a store of grain.
senses.example: The old stone garner stored the village's wheat through every hard winter.

senses.definition: An accumulation, supply, store, or hoard of something.
senses.example: The company keeps a garner of spare parts in the warehouse for emergencies.

senses.definition: To reap grain, gather it up, and store it in a granary.
senses.example: Farmers garnered the wheat before the early autumn rains ruined the harvest.

senses.definition: To gather, amass, hoard, as if harvesting grain.
senses.example: She garnered praise from reviewers for her debut novel this year.

senses.definition: To earn; to get; to accumulate or acquire (attitudes, reputations, or actions from others) by some effort or due to some fact.
senses.example: To garner support

senses.definition: (rare) To gather or become gathered; to accumulate or become accumulated; to become stored.
senses.example: Over the years, small savings garnered quietly in the account until we could buy a car.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To gather, earn, or win something such as support, praise, attention, or votes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, GAR. The second syllable is a single rhotic r sound, like the 'er' in 'water,' not a separate 'ner' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests effort or merit leading to a good result.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use garner in news reports, political writing, reviews, and business reports, such as garner support or garner attention. In casual speech, people usually say get, earn, or win. Garner is best in writing or formal presentations, where it sounds precise.

distinctions.note: Earn implies deserving something through work, while garner can describe gathering attention or support that comes from many sources.
Gather is neutral and general, while garner suggests collecting something valuable and prized.

examples.everyday: Her new podcast is starting to garner a lot of attention online.
examples.professional: The proposal garnered strong support from the engineering leads, so we can move forward.
examples.analytical: The argument garnered respect among scholars because it weighed evidence from several disciplines rather than a single source.

nuance.analogy: Like a farmer gathering grain into a barn, one piece at a time, until there is a full harvest.
nuance.etymology: From Old French grenier, from Latin granarium, 'granary,' the place where grain is stored.
common_mistakes: Using garner for everyday getting; say get or earn in casual speech.
Pronouncing the ending as 'ner' with a separate syllable; it is one rhotic syllable.

garner.etymology: From Middle English *gerner*, from Old French *gernier*, *guernier*, variant of *grenier*, from Latin *grānārium* (“granary”).

senses.definition: Garrulity.
senses.example: Her garrulousness at the dinner party meant nobody else got a word in edgewise.

core.definition: The quality of talking a great deal, especially about unimportant things, in a way that others find tiring.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllables are very light, and the -ul- is often a syllabic l with almost no vowel. The ending -ness is unstressed and ends in a weak 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies excessive, tiresome talk, though it can be mildly humorous in literature.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare and literary word. Americans would more naturally say talkativeness, chattiness or say that someone talks your ear off. Use garrulousness in writing or a formal critique of someone's style rather than in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Talkativeness is the common, neutral everyday word, while garrulousness is more formal and implies that the talk is excessive and tiresome.
Verbosity describes using too many words in writing or speech, whereas garrulousness refers to the habit of talking a lot.
Gregariousness means enjoying company and being sociable, which is positive; garrulousness is about talking too much and is usually negative.

examples.everyday: My uncle's garrulousness is fun at Thanksgiving, but after an hour everyone starts looking for an excuse to leave.
examples.professional: His garrulousness in the planning meeting ate up half the hour, so I asked the team to send updates in writing next time.
examples.analytical: The novel's narrator grows more troubling through a garrulousness that fills every silence with self-justification.

nuance.analogy: Garrulousness is like a radio that never turns off, filling every quiet moment with sound.
nuance.etymology: From Latin garrulus, talkative, from garrire, to chatter.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in ga-RUL-ous-ness; the stress is on the first syllable.
Confusing it with gregarious, which means sociable rather than talkative.

senses.definition: Comfortable, cosy, pleasant.
Friendly, genial, cheerful, easy-going.
senses.example: The little tavern felt wonderfully gemütlich, with warm lamps and friendly regulars.

core.definition: Cozy, warm and pleasant; relaxed, friendly and comfortable in a homey way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable 'MOOT'. The final sound is a soft 'kh' as in German, but many Americans say 'lish'; that is acceptable in casual speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: A German loanword used by some Americans, especially in describing cozy restaurants, homes or beer halls. Native English speakers might say 'cozy' or 'homey' in everyday talk; 'gemütlich' signals a German or Central European flavor.
word_family: Gemütlichkeit (noun, the quality of being gemütlich)

distinctions.note: Cozy is the common English word for warm and comfortable; gemütlich adds a German sense of friendly, sociable warmth.
Friendly describes a person's manner; gemütlich describes a place or atmosphere that feels warm and relaxed.

collocations: a gemütlich corner of the bar

examples.everyday: That little beer hall downtown is so gemütlich that we stayed until closing.
examples.professional: The offsite venue was chosen for its gemütlich feel, which made the strategy session less formal.
examples.analytical: The author describes the Bavarian inn as gemütlich, implying a social warmth that is more than physical comfort.

nuance.analogy: Like a sweater and a warm kitchen on a cold evening, where people relax and talk freely.
nuance.etymology: From German gemütlich, related to Gemüt, 'mind, disposition, temperament'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a verb or noun, when it is an adjective.
Pronouncing the u as in 'gem' rather than the German 'ü' sound, which Americans often approximate with 'oo'.

gemütlich.etymology: from Middle High German *gemüetlich*, from *gemüet* (“mind, mentality”) + *-lich* (“-ly”), equivalent to *Gemüt* + *lich*.

related: Gemütlichkeit (noun, the quality of being gemütlich)

senses.definition: A store which sells a large variety of useful things, without specializing highly in any particular type of merchandise, and which is not departmentalized.
senses.example: We bought birdseed, batteries, and fishing hooks at the old general store downtown.

core.definition: A small shop, often in a rural town, that sells a wide variety of everyday goods such as food, tools and clothing.

pronunciation.tip: In a compound noun, stress falls on the first word, JEN, and the second word has lighter stress. Pronounce the r in store clearly, since American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Positive and nostalgic. It suggests small-town life, friendly service and a traditional way of shopping.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use general store for an old-fashioned rural shop, often in small towns, historic villages or tourist areas. Today, the term is also used for a rustic store that sells candy, souvenirs and local goods. It is not a big store with departments, so do not use it for a large retail chain.

distinctions.note: A convenience store is a small modern shop that sells snacks, drinks and often gas, while a general store is usually older, rural and sells a wider mix of goods.
A department store is large and organized into departments, while a general store is small and not departmentalized.

examples.everyday: We stopped at the general store in town for a bag of ice and some sunscreen.
examples.professional: Our rural market study tested whether a general store format could serve communities without a grocery chain.
examples.analytical: The general store embodied an older economy in which one shopkeeper supplied nearly everything a village needed.

nuance.analogy: A general store is like a Swiss Army knife of shops: it has a little of everything, though none of it is highly specialized.
nuance.etymology: General from Latin generalis, 'relating to a kind'; store from Old French estore, 'supply.'
common_mistakes: Using general store for a large chain store; the American word for that is department store or big-box store.
Confusing general store with convenience store, which is more modern and focuses on snacks and fuel.

senses.definition: Popularly or widely.
senses.example: It is generally known that the Earth is round.

senses.definition: As a rule; usually; typically; in most cases.
senses.example: I generally have a walk in the afternoon.

senses.definition: Without reference to specific details.
senses.example: Generally speaking …

senses.definition: In the general case, without exception; in all cases.
senses.example: It is generally true that the angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees.

senses.definition: Collectively; as a whole; without omissions.
senses.example: Taken generally, the survey results show that most customers were satisfied with delivery times.

core.definition: Usually or in most cases; as a general rule, though there may be exceptions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on JEN. Americans say the middle syllable very quickly, often with a syllabic r, and the final -ly is a clear lee sound, not lay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it softens an absolute claim and sounds reasonable and measured.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use generally constantly in everyday speech to soften a statement: 'I generally wake up at six.' It works well in meetings or with friends when you want to avoid absolutes. It usually goes before the main verb in ordinary sentences, as in 'I generally agree.' 'Generally speaking' is also common and natural.

distinctions.note: Usually is about frequency in everyday talk; generally can also signal an overall pattern with exceptions.
Typically emphasizes what is standard or characteristic of a type; generally emphasizes an overall tendency without an exact rule.

examples.everyday: I generally grab a coffee after my morning run, but I skip it when I'm running late.
examples.professional: The team generally deploys updates on Tuesdays, so let's plan the release around that.
examples.analytical: Generally, moral obligation follows from the capacity to act, though philosophers disagree about the exceptions.

nuance.analogy: Generally is like a weather forecast: it tells you the overall pattern, not the exact temperature at every minute.
nuance.etymology: From general, from Latin generalis, plus -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing generally with generic; generally describes frequency or overall scope, while generic means ordinary or unbranded.
Mispronouncing it with an extra syllable, as JEN-er-al-ly; the usual form is quick and reduced in the middle.
Using generally to mean a general idea in formal writing where 'in general' or 'broadly' is more precise.

senses.definition: In a manner characterized by gentleness.
senses.example: She spoke gently to the frightened child in the emergency room.

senses.definition: Without strong force or quickness: softly, lightly.
senses.example: He set the vase down gently so it would not crack.

senses.definition: In a gentle manner; to a gentle degree.
senses.example: The coach pushed the team, but only gently, to avoid burnout.

senses.definition: Quietly: without much noise or motion.
senses.example: She closed the nursery door gently so the baby would keep sleeping.

senses.definition: (historical) From a gentle or high-class family.
senses.example: gently born
senses.label: historical

core.definition: In a soft, kind or careful way, without much force or speed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. In fast speech the t is often dropped or flapped, so it sounds like JEN-lee. Do not use a hard g as in 'get'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies care, patience and restraint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gently for touch, speech and handling: Gently close the door, or Gently press the button. Gently used is a standard phrase in online listings for secondhand items. It can also mean slowly or on a slope, as in a gently sloping hill.

distinctions.note: Softly describes sound or volume or a quiet, soft touch. Gently is broader and includes care in behavior.
Lightly is about weight or pressure. Gently includes kindness and care as well.
Kindly describes the intention or attitude of the person. Gently describes the manner of the action.

examples.everyday: Could you gently close the door? The baby just fell asleep.
examples.professional: I'd gently push back on that timeline before we commit to it with the client.
examples.analytical: The author gently challenges the assumption that efficiency and fairness always pull in the same direction.

nuance.analogy: Acting gently is like carrying a full cup of coffee across a crowded room: slow, steady and careful.
nuance.etymology: From gentle with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing gently with gentile, a different word.
Pronouncing the middle consonant cluster too strongly; the t is light in American speech.

senses.definition: To be delighted by; to be amused by.
senses.example: I really got a kick out of that clown's juggling act.

core.definition: To enjoy something a lot or find it funny or entertaining.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'kick' as the key word. 'A' and 'of' reduce to 'uh', and in fast speech 'out of' sounds like 'owt uv'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and playful; it describes amusement or pleasure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for things that amuse or please you, especially in a light, casual way: 'My dad gets a kick out of his grandkids' videos.' A natural reply is 'Me too' or 'I can see why.' Use it for things you find entertaining, not for serious matters.

distinctions.note: Enjoy is a general word for liking something, while get a kick out of suggests amusement and a bit of excitement.
Be into means you are keen on a hobby or topic; get a kick out of describes finding something fun or funny in the moment.

collocations: get a kick out of it
get a kick out of watching
really get a kick out of
get a kick out of teasing
kids get a kick out of

examples.everyday: My kids get a kick out of the way our dog chases his tail.
examples.professional: Our team got a kick out of the bug report that blamed the printer for everything.
examples.analytical: Readers may get a kick out of satire, yet its real purpose is to unsettle the very assumptions that amuse them.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden burst of laughter that catches you off guard, the pleasure arrives quickly and lifts the mood.
common_mistakes: Using 'to' instead of 'out of', as in 'get a kick to'.
Pronouncing 'a' as a full 'ay' instead of a reduced 'uh'.

conversation.text: My kids get a kick out of watching me try to dance.
I think you'll get a kick out of this video.
He gets a kick out of solving tricky data problems.

senses.definition: To move into (an object), such that one ends up inside it.
senses.example: She got into the car.

senses.definition: To put on (an item of clothing).
senses.example: I'm soaking wet. I need to get into some dry clothes.

senses.definition: To reach into or interact with (an object).
senses.example: The small child got into everything.

senses.definition: To become involved or interested in (a discussion, issue, or activity); to come to enjoy (something).
senses.example: He got into politics.

senses.definition: To enter (an unfavorable state).
senses.example: How did we get into such a mess?

senses.definition: To cause to behave uncharacteristically; to possess.
senses.example: I don't know what's gotten into that child.

senses.definition: To interrogate in order to arrive at a deeper understanding.
To penetrate (someone) sexually.
To owe money to (someone); to become involved in something unsavory.
senses.example: He's gotten into the gang to the tune of five grand.

senses.definition: To argue about or discuss (something).
senses.example: Oh let's not get into that again.

core.definition: To enter something, such as a car, a room, or clothing, or to become involved in an activity or interest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on IN, and 'into' is often reduced to a quick 'IN-tuh' in fast speech. Keep the vowel short, as in 'bit', not a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the meaning depends on context, and the phrase is harmless in most uses.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'get into the car' or 'get into bed', and they also use 'get into' for interests and habits, as in 'get into golf.' 'Get in' is the common form for cars and small vehicles, while 'get into' suits both physical and figurative uses. A natural reply to 'Get into the car' is 'Okay, I'm coming.'

distinctions.note: Enter is formal and used for buildings, systems, or data; get into is everyday and used for cars, clothing, and interests.
Get in is most common for cars and small vehicles, while get into works in a wider range of contexts.

examples.everyday: Hurry up and get into the car, or we'll miss the first half of the movie.
examples.professional: Before the workshop, you should get into the habit of documenting every model change in the repository.
examples.analytical: Philosophers often get into the question of whether moral facts exist independently of human minds.

nuance.analogy: Like slipping into a warm bath: you move your whole body inside and settle into the space.
nuance.etymology: 'Get' comes from Old Norse geta; 'into' combines in and to from Old English.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'get into' (enter) with 'get on' (board a bus or train)
Saying 'get into' with two equal stresses, when 'into' should be reduced
Using 'get into' for a formal building entry where 'enter' is more precise

senses.definition: To board or mount (something), especially a vehicle.
senses.example: Please get on the bus as quickly as possible.

senses.definition: To cope or manage (over time); to handle a situation; to perform or make progress.
senses.example: John is really getting on at work.

senses.definition: To progress (with); to move forward.
senses.example: It's time to get on with improving quality.

senses.definition: To move forward so as to approach a deadline or become late in the day.
senses.example: Time is getting on. We need to hurry up or we'll miss our flight.

senses.definition: To approach (a value, level, point in time, etc.) (see also getting on).
senses.example: The cost was getting on for a thousand pounds.

senses.definition: To become old.
senses.example: My parents are visibly getting on (in years) these days.

senses.definition: To commence (an action).
senses.example: Go get on to cleaning the floors, the others have already started.

senses.definition: Synonym of have on (“to wear”).
senses.example: She got on her red dress and headed out for the party.

senses.definition: To have sex; to be sexually promiscuous.
senses.example: Everyone at the party knew those two were going to get on before the night ended.

senses.definition: To do drugs; to get drunk; to buy drugs; to regularly use drugs.
senses.example: Some of the guys in my dorm would get on every weekend and skip class.

senses.definition: To observe or notice.
senses.example: Get on that guy!

senses.definition: Expresses surprise or disbelief.
senses.example: Get on! You actually won the lottery? I can't believe it.

core.definition: To board a bus, train or plane, or to continue or make progress with something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ON. Many Americans pronounce it /ɑn/, like 'con', because of the cot-caught merger, and the t in 'get' is often flapped or reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a routine travel or work action.
nuance.usage_note: Very common for transit: 'Get on the train before the doors close.' 'Get on with it' tells someone to stop delaying. 'Get on well with' someone means have a good relationship. The interjection 'Get on!' meaning 'No way' is mainly British; Americans say 'No way' or 'Come on.'

distinctions.note: Board is more formal and common in announcements; get on is everyday speech.
Get on is used for buses, trains and planes; get in is used for cars and taxis.

examples.everyday: Hurry, get on the bus before it leaves without us!
examples.professional: Let's get on the call first, then we can review the slides together.
examples.analytical: The author asks whether a reader can get on board with a thesis that never states its assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like stepping onto a moving escalator: you join the motion already underway.
nuance.etymology: Get from Old Norse geta; on from Old English on.
common_mistakes: Saying 'get on the car' for a car; say 'get in the car'.
Using 'get on' for 'get on the phone'; say 'get on a call' or 'join the call'.

conversation.text: Hurry up and get on the bus!
We got on the wrong train and ended up in Brooklyn.
Let me get on my laptop and check the schedule.
Let's get on with the meeting, we're behind.
Get on the bus at Main Street and ride it to the end.
We got on the plane right before they closed the door.
Let me get on the call; it's starting now.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to ghosts or spirits.
senses.example: a ghostly figure with a hood

senses.definition: Spooky; frightening.
senses.example: A ghostly hush fell.

core.definition: Relating to ghosts or spirits; spooky, eerie, or pale like a ghost.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, GOHST. The 'st' cluster is clear, and the final syllable is a light 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative: it suggests something eerie or frightening.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ghostly mostly in writing and descriptions, such as a ghostly figure in a novel or a ghostly glow in a photo. In everyday speech they more often say spooky or creepy. The word can also describe a faint, pale appearance.

distinctions.note: Ghastly means horrible or very bad, while ghostly means relating to ghosts or eerie.
Spooky is casual and common in speech; ghostly is more literary and descriptive.

examples.everyday: The fog rolled in over the lake and made the old boat look ghostly.
examples.professional: The unused server room had a ghostly hum from the cooling fans running with no load.
examples.analytical: The novel's ghostly figures serve less as supernatural events than as images of a past the characters cannot escape.

nuance.analogy: Like a faint pencil sketch that seems to float off the page.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gaestlic, spiritual, from gaest, spirit or ghost, with the suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing ghostly with ghastly, which means horrible or very bad.
Using ghostly for a large, solid object; it describes a spooky or pale appearance.

ghostly.etymology: From Middle English *gostly*, *gastlich*, from Old English *gāstlīċ* (“spiritual, holy, clerical, ghastly, ghostly, spectral”), from **gaistalīk* (“spiritual”), equivalent to *ghost* + *ly*.

core.definition: The father of Abidan, the leader of the tribe of Benjamin named in the wilderness census in the Book of Numbers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the final -i is pronounced like "eye". The first vowel is short, like the i in "sit".

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Gideoni is used almost only in Bible study, genealogy, or discussion of the Book of Numbers. Most Americans will not know the name, so it is safe to say it only when you are talking about Scripture or a specific passage.

distinctions.note: Gideon is the famous judge of Judges; Gideoni is a minor figure in Numbers and the two names should not be confused.

examples.everyday: Do you remember who Gideoni was? I always mix him up with the judge Gideon.
examples.professional: In the Numbers census lists, Abidan appears as the son of Gideoni, the leader for Benjamin.
examples.analytical: The genealogical notice naming Gideoni as Abidan's father anchors Benjamin's leadership in the wilderness organization of the tribes.

nuance.analogy: Like a name in a family tree that appears once in a long list, important only to the record it sits in.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Gidh'oni, related to the name Gideon; the exact meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing Gideoni with Gideon, the judge in Judges 6 to 8.
Stressing the first syllable (GID-ee-oh-ny) instead of the second.
nuance.biblical_note: Gideoni (Hebrew Gidh'oni) is the father of Abidan, who is named as the leader of the tribe of Benjamin in the wilderness census (Numbers 1:11). Abidan appears again in Numbers 2:22, 7:60, 7:65 and 10:24, where his family's role in the camp and offerings is recorded. The passages show his father only as a genealogical link.

senses.definition: A single serving of wine, ordered by the glass rather than the bottle.

core.definition: One serving of wine poured into a glass, ordered by the glass rather than the whole bottle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on wine, and of is reduced to a weak uh sound, so it sounds like "glass-uv-WINE". Glass has a short a, as in cat.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it is friendly and casual, often used in social settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say "a glass of wine" when ordering or offering a drink, such as "Can I get a glass of red?" At restaurants, "by the glass" is the more natural phrasing on menus. A common reply to "Would you like a glass of wine?" is "Sure, thanks!" or "Just one for me, please."

distinctions.note: A bottle is the whole container, often shared; a glass is one serving for a single person.
A glass alone is just the container; a glass of wine specifies the drink.

examples.everyday: Could I get a glass of white wine, please?
examples.professional: Let's grab a glass of wine after the conference session and talk about the proposal.
examples.analytical: The philosopher used the image of a single glass of wine to illustrate the difference between pleasure and excess.

nuance.analogy: Like a single slice from a pie: one portion, not the whole thing.
nuance.etymology: Glass comes from Old English glæs; of is from Old English of, meaning from or belonging to.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing of with a full vowel, as in "ohv"; it is usually uhv.
Saying "a wine glass" when you mean the drink; a wine glass is the container, while a glass of wine is the drink.

conversation.text: I'll have a glass of wine with dinner.
Would you like a glass of wine or the whole bottle?
She had one glass of wine and switched to water.

senses.definition: An appearance of light, especially one which is indistinct or small, or short-lived.
senses.example: A faint gleam of light showed under the door of the empty church.

senses.definition: An indistinct sign of something; a glimpse or hint.
senses.example: The rescue workers preserved a gleam of optimism that the trapped miners might still survive.

senses.definition: A bright, but intermittent or short-lived, appearance of something.
senses.example: A sudden gleam of hope crossed her face when the phone finally rang.

senses.definition: A look of joy or liveliness on one's face.
senses.example: The child's face held a gleam of delight as the puppy ran toward her.

senses.definition: Sometimes as hot gleam: a warm ray of sunlight; also, a period of warm weather, for instance, between showers of rain.
senses.example: After three cold weeks, a gleam of warm sunshine finally lifted the town's spirits.

senses.definition: Brightness or shininess; radiance, splendor.
senses.example: The polished silver gleam of the trophy caught everyone's attention across the room.

senses.definition: Chiefly in conjunction with an adverb: to cause (light) to shine.
senses.example: He gleamed his flashlight across the dark water to find the dock.

senses.definition: To shine, especially in an indistinct or intermittent manner; to glisten, to glitter.
senses.example: The wet cobblestones gleamed under the streetlamps after the evening rain.

senses.definition: To be strongly but briefly apparent.
senses.example: Hope gleamed in his mind for a moment before the doctor's results came back.

core.definition: A brief, faint flash or shine of light, or a small hint of something hopeful.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a long 'ee' vowel. Do not shorten it to the vowel of 'gym', and remember that it differs from glean, which is also pronounced GLEEN.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral: it suggests a small, welcome sign of light or hope.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gleam in everyday talk for light on water, metal, or eyes, and for small signs of hope, as in 'a gleam of hope.' It is more common in writing and storytelling than in quick conversation. Because the sense is faint, it works well when something is only barely visible.

distinctions.note: A glint is a quick, sharp flash of light, while a gleam is a steadier but faint shine.
A glimmer is fainter and often used for hope or understanding, while gleam can describe either light or a sign of something.

examples.everyday: I saw a gleam of sunlight through the clouds on the way home.
examples.professional: The new dashboard shows a gleam of improvement in customer retention, though the trend is not yet clear.
examples.analytical: A faint gleam of order emerges from the poem's fragmented structure, suggesting meaning beneath apparent chaos.

nuance.analogy: A gleam is like a fish's scales flickering in a stream: there, then gone.
nuance.etymology: From Old English glæm 'brightness, splendor'.
common_mistakes: Confusing gleam with glean, which means to gather leftover crops or information.
Using gleam for a long, strong light; the word suggests something faint or brief.

gleam.etymology: From Middle English *glem*, *gleam*, *gleme* (“shaft of light; reflected light; radiance; something ephemeral”), from Old English *glǣm* (“gleam”), from **glaimi* (“brightness; splendour”), from Proto-Indo-European **ǵʰley-* (“to shine”).

senses.definition: Showing all great circles as straight lines, and thus preserving the shortest distances between any two locations.
senses.example: The navigator plotted the route on a gnomonic chart, where great circles appear as straight lines.

core.definition: Relating to a map projection in which all great circles appear as straight lines, so shortest routes can be read directly from the map.

pronunciation.tip: The initial g is silent, so start with 'no'. The stress falls on the second syllable, MAH, and the final -ic is short, not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly hear this word in aviation, shipping, cartography, and geometry courses. Pilots and navigators say 'great-circle route' in everyday talk and reserve 'gnomonic' for the map type itself. Do not confuse it with 'gnomic', which describes a pithy saying.

distinctions.note: A Mercator map keeps angles accurate and shows rhumb lines as straight, but it badly distorts distances near the poles, whereas a gnomonic map shows great circles as straight lines.
'Gnomic' describes a wise saying or aphorism, while 'gnomonic' is a technical term about map projections and sundials.

collocations: great-circle route on a gnomonic map

examples.everyday: My brother is a pilot, and he showed me why our flight path curves when you look at a gnomonic map.
examples.professional: For the Arctic shipping study, we plotted the candidate routes on a gnomonic projection so the great-circle paths appear as straight lines.
examples.analytical: A gnomonic projection makes shortest paths visible as straight lines, but it sacrifices angle and area accuracy, so its value depends on the question being asked.

nuance.analogy: Like a sheet of paper touching a globe at one point, where the shortest routes look like straight lines drawn across it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek gnōmonikos, relating to a gnomon, the pointer or carpenter's square used to cast shadows.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'gnomonic' with 'gnomic', which means pithy and wise.
Saying the silent g as in 'g-NOH-mik'.

gnomonic.etymology: From Latin *gnōmonicus*, Ancient Greek *γνωμονικός* (“judging by rule”).

senses.definition: Charming, pleasing qualities.
senses.example: The Princess brought grace to an otherwise dull and boring party.

senses.definition: A short prayer of thanks before or after a meal.
senses.example: It has become less common to say grace before having dinner.

senses.definition: In the games of patience or solitaire: a special move that is normally against the rules.
senses.example: My grandmother allowed one grace in solitaire, but only when the game was nearly lost.

senses.definition: Elegant movement; elegance of movement; balance or poise.
senses.example: The dancer moved with grace and strength.

senses.definition: An allowance of time granted to a debtor during which they are free of at least part of their normal obligations towards the creditor.
senses.example: The repayment of the loan starts after a three-year grace.

senses.definition: Favor, sanction or beneficence.
senses.example: The minister has extended his grace to our effort.

senses.definition: Free and undeserved favor from God; unmerited divine assistance given to humans for their regeneration or sanctification, or for resisting sin.
senses.example: divine grace

senses.definition: An act or decree of the governing body of an English university.
senses.example: The university senate passed a grace that extended the library's opening hours.

senses.definition: A grace note.
senses.example: The pianist added a quick grace before the melody's final note.

senses.definition: To adorn; to decorate; to embellish and dignify.
senses.example: He graced the room with his presence.

senses.definition: To dignify or raise by an act of favor; to honor.
senses.example: The governor graced our small library with a visit and a signed photograph.

senses.definition: To supply with heavenly grace.
senses.example: Pray that God graces your family with peace and strength through this difficult season.

senses.definition: To add grace notes, cadenzas, etc. to.
senses.example: She graced the slow melody with trills and ornaments, adding cadenzas on the repeat.

core.definition: Smooth, elegant movement, polite goodwill, or a short prayer before a meal; in theology, God's free, undeserved favor toward humans.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a long 'ay' sound. The American r after 'g' needs the tongue pulled back, and the ending is a clear 's,' not 'z.'

nuance.connotation: Positive: kindness, elegance or divine favor. 'Fall from grace' is negative, and 'saving grace' is positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'grace' for elegance ('She handled it with grace'), for a mealtime prayer ('Let's say grace'), and in religion for God's unearned favor. 'Grace period' is common in business and finance. 'Amazing Grace' is one of the best-known American hymns.

distinctions.note: Mercy is not giving someone the punishment they deserve; grace is giving a gift they did not earn.
Elegance is refined style, while grace is smooth, easy movement or manner.
Favor is a general act of kindness; grace is a free gift that is not earned, especially from God.
Courtesy is polite behavior, while grace suggests kindness that goes beyond what is required.

examples.everyday: Before we eat, would you like to say grace?
examples.professional: The bank gave us a ten-day grace period before charging a late fee.
